title: Macramé hammock chair swing
subtitle: A full-size knotted cotton chair suspended from a single ceiling point
excerpt: A macramé hammock chair is a full-size seat formed from a knotted cotton cord body suspended from a single wooden spreader bar and a ceiling hook. The finished chair holds up to 100 kg and requires about 80 m of 5 mm or 6 mm cotton cord. It is a demanding project that tests consistent tension and knot sequence over several sessions.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from traditional macramé craft practice and modern hammock-chair construction guides. Hanging chair construction in knotted cord is a well-established structural macramé project; the specific pattern here is synthesised from standard guild workshop teaching.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat symmetrical knot made with two working cords around two or more filler cords. The structural backbone of a macramé hammock chair.
A simple wrapping knot where the working cord passes over and under a filler cord and through its own loop.
A chain of repeated knots, usually square knots, worked vertically to create a structural column.
The mounting knot used to attach cords to the spreader ring at the start of the chair.

content.text: A macramé hammock chair is built from
square-knot
panels and
sennit
columns of rope that support a person's weight from a single ceiling suspension point. Cords are mounted with
lark's head knots
to a 15 to 20 cm metal or wooden ring at the top, and the knotted body flares outward below it to form the seat. The chair requires consistent
half-hitch
and square-knot tension across 40 or more cord pairs over 50 to 60 cm of knotting. Structural confidence in all the foundational knots is a prerequisite.

attrs.title: Structural safety
attrs.body: Test load capacity before sitting. Check the ceiling fixing supports 200 kg minimum. Inspect cord for wear at the ring before every use.

items.name: 5 mm or 6 mm 3-ply cotton macramé cord
Solid metal ring, 15 to 20 cm diameter (rated for load bearing)
Wooden spreader bar or second ring for the seat base
Heavy ceiling hook and appropriate fixings
Large metal carabiner or swivel hook

content.text: Method
Step 1: Mount the suspension ring

Cut 40 cords, each 2 m long. Fold each in half and mount with lark's head knots around the suspension ring, packing the knots tightly around the full circumference of the ring. This produces 80 working ends hanging below the ring. Divide the cords into groups of four for square-knot working.
Step 2: Form the cone above the seat

Work 8 to 10 rows of square knots in an alternating pattern, starting immediately below the ring. The alternating pattern produces a net-like diamond structure that flares outward as the rows progress. Keep the tension even across all rows; inconsistent tension at this stage creates an asymmetric seat that will list to one side when occupied.
Step 3: Create the seat base

Gather the cord ends at the bottom of the knotted body and pass them through the spreader bar (or second ring) to form the seat base. Divide the cords into groups and work a row of square knots immediately below the spreader bar to hold the cords in position. The seat base should be about 50 cm across for a standard sitting position.
Step 4: Add suspension cords and hanging

Attach three or four long cords from the spreader bar up to the suspension ring to maintain the seat angle at rest. The chair should hang at a slight backward lean (about 15 degrees from vertical) for comfortable sitting. Adjust the length of the suspension cords to achieve this angle. Attach the whole assembly to the ceiling hook via a carabiner or swivel hook.
Step 5: Test and trim

Before sitting in the chair, load-test it by hanging a weight equal to or greater than your body weight from the seat for at least 10 minutes. Check all knots, the ring, and the ceiling fixing under load. Once the test is passed, trim the cord fringe below the seat to a consistent length.

items.problem: The seat is too narrow and uncomfortable for sitting
items.cause: The spreader bar or second ring is too small, or the knotted body did not flare sufficiently
items.fix: Use a wider spreader bar (at least 50 cm) and leave a generous gap between knots so the body can flare outward.

items.problem: The chair lists severely to one side when occupied
items.cause: The knot tension on one side of the chair is significantly tighter than the other, pulling that side upward
items.fix: Check all square knots across the width and compare tension by squeezing each knot gently. Loosen overly tight knots carefully with a blunt tool before the chair is used again.
